subject: 문자 없는 사회의 기억 전달
title: How societies without writing kept their past
content: Societies that never developed writing are often described as having no history, as though the absence of documents entailed the absence of a past. The description confuses a record with a medium. What such communities lacked was not memory but paper, and they built other instruments to carry what mattered forward. Genealogies were recited at fixed occasions, boundaries were encoded in the sequence of a journey, and obligations between families were preserved in the order of gifts exchanged at a marriage. Each of these devices attached information to an action that people had reason to repeat, so the record was rehearsed rather than stored. This arrangement has properties that written archives lack. Because the account is performed before an audience that also knows it, errors are corrected in public, and a speaker who departs from the accepted version is challenged on the spot. A document, by contrast, can drift uncontested for centuries once it has been copied. Yet the same feature limits what oral transmission can hold. Details that no longer serve anyone tend to fall away, and the past therefore remains continuous with present concerns instead of standing apart from them as a separate object of study. Historians who work with such traditions have learned to read this shaping rather than to lament it. When a lineage compresses several generations into one, the compression itself indicates which ancestors carried authority, and the omission becomes evidence. Treating the account as a defective chronicle discards precisely the information it was built to convey, and it imports a standard from a technology those communities never adopted.

subject: 교역망이 만든 도시
title: Cities that trade built
content: The conventional account of urban origins begins with agriculture. Farmers produced a surplus, the surplus supported specialists, and the specialists gathered into towns. This sequence is orderly and it fits several regions, but it does not fit others, and the exceptions are instructive rather than marginal. Several early cities arose at points where routes converged rather than where soil was rich, and their inhabitants imported much of what they ate. What concentrated people there was exchange itself, since a place where many parties met acquired advantages that no single producer could supply. Storage, measurement, arbitration, and credit all became easier when strangers had to meet repeatedly in the same location. Consider what a merchant needs in order to accept a promise from someone he may not see again. He needs a way to record the obligation, a third party who will enforce it, and a shared standard by which goods are compared. None of these can be carried on a journey; they must exist at a fixed point. Cities of this kind therefore grew as institutions before they grew as populations, and their earliest monumental structures were often warehouses and courts rather than palaces. The distinction matters for how we interpret decline. When such a settlement was abandoned, the cause was frequently a shift in the routes rather than a failure of its fields, and archaeologists who look only at local agriculture will find no explanation. The city was never sustained by its hinterland alone, and it ended when the traffic that made it necessary moved elsewhere.

subject: 친족 용어가 드러내는 사회 구조
title: What kinship words disclose
content: Every language supplies terms for relatives, and the terms differ in ways that are not merely verbal. Some systems give a single word to the father and to the father's brother while distinguishing the mother's brother sharply. Others separate siblings by relative age but ignore the distinction between cousins and siblings entirely. These patterns are not random, and they correspond closely to how obligations are distributed within the community. Where a word is shared, duties are typically shared as well, and where a word divides, something practical usually divides with it. This correspondence gives anthropologists a method. Because kinship terms are learned early and used constantly, they change slowly and preserve arrangements that may no longer be practiced, much as an old street plan survives beneath a rebuilt city. A society that has adopted new rules of inheritance may continue to speak as though the older rules held, and the discrepancy between what people say and what they do becomes a record of the transition. The method has limits that its early practitioners underestimated. Terminology constrains conduct less tightly than they supposed, and individuals negotiate around categories rather than obeying them. A term may also spread through contact without carrying its original arrangements, so a shared word can indicate borrowing instead of common descent. The words are therefore evidence rather than proof, and they must be read alongside what people actually do with property, residence, and marriage before any structure can be inferred from them.

subject: 연대기와 사료 비판
title: Reading chronicles against themselves
content: A chronicle presents itself as a record of what happened, and for a long time historians treated it accordingly, extracting events and discarding the rest as ornament. Source criticism reversed that priority. Its founding observation is that every chronicle was written by someone for someone, and that the shape of the account carries information the author did not intend to supply. A monastery that recorded floods and royal deaths but ignored a famine reveals what it considered worth remembering, and that judgment is itself a historical fact. This shift changed which questions could be asked. Instead of asking whether a report is true, the historian asks who was in a position to know, what the writer stood to gain, and which conventions governed the form. A miracle account, for instance, may be worthless as testimony about an event while remaining excellent evidence about the expectations of its audience. Nothing is discarded; material that failed one test is redirected to another. The approach carries its own risk. If every text is read primarily as an expression of interest, then the question of what actually occurred can quietly disappear, and the past dissolves into a sequence of representations. Careful practitioners resist that conclusion. They hold that bias is an obstacle to be measured rather than a reason to abandon the attempt, and that comparing several interested accounts remains the most reliable route to what happened, because the interests rarely coincide.

subject: 의례의 반복이 만드는 공동체
title: Repetition before belief
content: Observers have long assumed that a ceremony expresses convictions its participants already hold, so that the ritual is an outward sign of an inward state. Extended fieldwork makes this assumption difficult to sustain. Participants often disagree about what a rite means, offer explanations that contradict one another, or decline to interpret it at all, insisting that the actions were performed correctly and that correctness was the point. Belief, on closer inspection, was frequently supplied by the observer rather than found among those observed. An alternative account reverses the direction. Repeated action does not follow from conviction; it produces the dispositions from which conviction later emerges. Standing, kneeling, and reciting together establish a bodily habit of participation, and significance attaches afterward to whatever explanation the community makes available. The absence of shared interpretation then ceases to be puzzling, because agreement was never located in the interpretations. It was located in the practice, which everyone could perform without agreeing about it. This reversal reaches well beyond religion. Institutions of every sort depend on repeated forms that participants could not readily justify, from the procedures of a court to the conventions of a seminar, and in each case the form accomplishes what no statement of purpose could. Reforms that address only the stated rationale therefore tend to fail, since they leave the practice intact and the practice was doing the work. Ritual remains open to criticism, but criticism aimed at what participants believe usually misses, because the beliefs are downstream of the actions rather than their source.

subject: 가축화는 누가 누구를 길들였나
title: Who domesticated whom
content: Domestication is usually narrated as a human achievement, in which our ancestors selected useful animals and bent their descendants to human purposes. The narrative is not false, yet it obscures how much the relationship altered the people who entered it. Herders became bound to the seasonal needs of their animals, moving where the pasture required rather than where they preferred, and farmers who kept cattle acquired obligations that structured the working year. The species that were taken in reshaped the daily lives of those who took them. Biologically the exchange was mutual in a stricter sense. Populations of cattle, sheep, and dogs expanded enormously under human protection, spreading into ranges they could never have occupied alone, while their keepers underwent changes of their own. The ability to digest milk in adulthood arose independently in several herding populations, and it spread rapidly wherever dairying was practiced. A trait of human bodies was therefore selected by a practice that animals made possible. None of this implies that animals chose anything, and the asymmetry of power is not in doubt. What the evidence undermines is the assumption that domestication was an act performed on a passive subject. It was a long entanglement in which each party altered the conditions under which the other lived, and reading it as a one-sided conquest conceals the reciprocal pressures that made the arrangement durable enough to reshape both.

subject: 달력과 시간의 표준화
title: The calendar as an instrument of rule
content: A calendar looks like a description of nature, and in one respect it is, since it tracks the return of seasons and the phases of the moon. Yet no astronomical fact determines where a year should begin, how a month should be divided, or which days should be set aside. Those decisions are made by whoever has authority to make them, and they are enforced because coordination requires that everyone use the same reckoning. The calendar is therefore an instrument of administration wearing the appearance of a natural law. Its administrative character becomes visible whenever the reckoning changes. Reforms that adjusted the count of days provoked resistance out of proportion to the inconvenience, because tenants owed rent on fixed dates, festivals anchored the agricultural year, and a shifted date moved obligations along with it. What appeared to be a quarrel about astronomy was a quarrel about who owed what to whom, and the parties understood this clearly even when they argued in technical language. Standardization also has a direction. A ruler who imposes a single calendar makes distant activity legible from the center, since taxes, courts, and campaigns can be scheduled without local negotiation. Communities that kept their own reckoning were correspondingly harder to govern, and they often defended it long after the practical cost of divergence had become severe. The calendar, in other words, was rarely neutral, and its adoption marked the reach of an authority rather than the discovery of a fact.

subject: 기술 전파는 왜 고르지 않았나
title: Why techniques travelled unevenly
content: It is tempting to assume that a useful technique will spread wherever people encounter it, so that the distribution of a tool records the extent of contact. The historical pattern is far less regular. Societies that knew of the wheel declined to use it for transport, ironworking arrived in some regions centuries after their neighbours had adopted it, and printing was known long before it was applied to books in several places. Contact was evidently not sufficient, and the reasons are worth examining rather than dismissing as conservatism. A technique is rarely a single object. It arrives embedded in a set of supporting arrangements, and it requires roads, draught animals, fuel, specialists, or a market before it repays the effort of adoption. Where those arrangements were absent, the tool remained a curiosity, and the community that declined it was making a defensible judgment about its own circumstances rather than failing to appreciate an advantage. The wheel is useless without surfaces it can roll on. There is a further consideration that purely practical accounts overlook. Adopting a technique often redistributes standing within a community, since it transfers advantage from those who command the older skill to those who master the new one. Resistance may therefore express an accurate assessment of who would lose, and its persistence indicates that the losers had enough influence to prevail. Diffusion, on this reading, is not a natural flow that obstacles occasionally block. It is an outcome that must be explained wherever it occurs.

subject: 무덤 부장품이 말하는 위계
title: Grave goods and ancient rank
content: Burials are among the richest sources we have for ancient societies that left no writing, and the goods buried with the dead have long served to measure rank. The reasoning looks plain. Where some graves of a given century hold imported metal and others hold nothing, the society that made them was divided. Yet the step from grave to rank rests on an assumption worth testing, namely that what went into the ground with a person marks what that person held while alive. Evidence from living communities unsettles that assumption. In some, the goods buried express the standing of the mourners rather than the dead, so a rich grave advertises the wealth of those who dug it. In others the most powerful elders are buried plainly, because display is reserved for those whom the community counts as dangerous or unfinished. A child's grave may then be the richest in the cemetery, and reading it as proof of inherited rank would invert what it meant. None of this makes ancient burials useless, and archaeologists have not set them aside. It obliges them to look for patterns across a whole cemetery rather than at single graves, and to seek support in house remains, in diet read from bone, and in the labour the tomb itself demanded. Where several measures agree, a claim about hierarchy grows firm. Where only the grave goods speak, it stays one reading among many.

subject: 구전 계보의 정확성과 그 한계
title: Remembered ancestors and the shape of descent
content: Oral genealogies can be strikingly exact. Reciters in some communities carry twenty generations of ancestors without pause, and where written records survive the names have at times been matched across several centuries. Such feats were once used to argue that memory is a reliable archive, and that documents merely made an older human capacity portable. The evidence is genuinely impressive, yet the argument claims more than it can carry. The difficulty is that a genealogy does work beyond remembering. It grounds claims to land, to office, and to marriage partners, so a line that no longer supports a claim tends to fade while a line that supports a contested one tends to grow. Recitations gathered decades apart show exactly this. Ancestors vanish once the families they justified have lost their fields, and new links appear when an alliance needs a common forebear. The account stays accurate about the present arrangement of kin, which is what it exists to state. Anthropologists therefore read such genealogies as maps of standing rather than as history, and the difference governs what may be drawn from them. Depth in generations marks the antiquity a group claims, not the antiquity it holds, and a sudden shortening records a defeat rather than a death. Read as chronicle the recitation misleads. Read as a claim about who belongs with whom, it is unusually direct evidence, and it tells us what documents seldom do.

subject: 문자의 발명은 회계에서 시작됐다
title: Ancient writing began with accounts
content: Stories about the origin of writing often begin with poetry, as though the wish to record grew from a wish to preserve tales. The oldest tablets suggest otherwise. They are almost wholly administrative: measures of grain, counts of animals, debts owed, and rations handed out. Narrative texts appear centuries later, and by then the notation had been in use for many generations. Writing seems to have arisen in order to track things rather than to say anything. The sequence makes sense once the practical problem is weighed. A household can remember what it owes and to whom, but a temple that gathers from hundreds of farmers and feeds hundreds of dependents cannot. Its officials change, its dealings overlap, and its quarrels need a record that outlives whoever saw the first bargain struck. The clay tokens that came before full writing answer just this need, and they grew under the pressure of scale rather than of expression. What followed was not bound to happen. A notation good enough for quantities does not become good enough for sentences on its own, and the extension called for signs that stood for sounds rather than for things. That step was taken in some ancient centres and not in others, and where it was not, elaborate accounting survived for centuries without ever recording speech. The capacity we treat as one invention was assembled in stages, and only the last of them yielded literature.

subject: 지도 제작과 영토 관념
title: Mapping and the idea of territory
content: A modern political map shows the world divided into areas of uniform colour, each bounded by a line and each belonging entirely to one authority. The image is so familiar that it appears to record an obvious fact about how power is organized. Historically, however, this arrangement is unusual, and for most of the past authority was exercised over people and routes rather than over continuous surfaces. A ruler collected from communities that acknowledged him, and the land between them belonged to nobody in particular. Cartography did not simply describe the shift to bounded territory; it helped bring the shift about. Once a border was drawn, it had to be located on the ground, and the survey that located it produced records of who lived where and what they owed. Populations that had previously moved between several patrons found themselves assigned to one, and practices that depended on ambiguity became irregularities to be corrected. The map made a certain kind of claim possible, and the claim then reshaped what it purported to depict. This history explains why disputes about boundaries are so intractable. The parties are not merely disagreeing about where a line falls; they are frequently working with incompatible ideas about what a line does. Where one side asserts exclusive control over an area, the other may be asserting a relationship with particular communities that the area happens to contain. Treating the disagreement as a technical problem of surveying therefore misses what is actually at issue, and it privileges one conception by presenting it as neutral procedure.
